hale_corvane.name: Abbot Hale Corvane
hale_corvane.role: abbot of the pilgrims' halt and former acolyte of Ahn-Solis
hale_corvane.personality: heavy, soft-voiced, carries guilt like a second stole; feeds crows and speaks to them as colleagues
hale_corvane.voice: liturgical cadence worn down by use; confessions disguised as small talk; long pauses before the true sentence

say: Hale Corvane, abbot of this halt, for want of anyone better. You carry the sun's mark on your hand. Do not hide it. The crows told me three days ago that a light-bearer was on the road.

A black bier passed here at the new moon. Wyvern-drawn, a rider before it, and on it a man in white who did not look at any of us. Every lantern on the pond went out as it went by. All forty-one, in a line.

The Chancellor was my teacher once. Before the temple fell, he taught me to read the stars. If you go up the climb, bring down the rider first. Wyverns hate lightning. Then go to the summit and look him in the face, because I never could.
The wind changed at noon. Forty-one lanterns on the pond lit themselves, one after another, from the left to the right, and not one pilgrim spoke. I fed the crow and told it that the vigil was over.
He gave you the shard, and he told you what the mark is. Yes. I suspected, and I never dared say it aloud. I am sorry. Not for the truth. For all the years that nobody told you.

Here is what the halt can give: the common purse, and every cure on the shelf. The road down to the Descent opens from the old chantry at the summit. Go with a clear head. A vessel is a thing that holds. It is not a thing that breaks, unless it is asked to.

lines.text: A vigil is a candle you promise to watch. The trouble begins when the candle outlives the one who made the promise.
The pond freezes to a hand's depth each winter and thaws to a hand's depth each spring. I have measured it for twenty years. It is the only prayer I never missed.
Crows are the best congregation. They arrive on time, they never cough, and they keep my secrets by forgetting them.
A wyvern cannot long abide a bolt from the clouds. Lightning in the wing, and the whole animal remembers it is a lizard of good size.
The Chancellor does not fall once. He fell in the old temple and rose. Be ready to strike him twice, and mean it both times.
I buried my faith in the pond the year the sun stopped answering. I dig it up in winter to see if it has changed. It never changes size.
Swordsman, carry a lightning charm if one can be found. A blade cannot reach a rider who will not come down.
Caster, your storm spells are the key to this road. Speak the thunder, and the sky will return what it borrowed.
Scout, the rider is quick, but a wyvern's wing has a seam under the shoulder. Aim there, and be patient.
Healer, the pilgrims would welcome a blessing before the climb. Most of them cannot remember a prayer. They will remember yours.
Senna keeps the third brazier and has not asked for anything in six days. I take that for a request, and an answer is still beyond me.
Harl studies the wyverns the way a physician studies a fever. I have never met a man who loved a monster so carefully.
Ilka tends the sick in the long house. She is not a sister of any order. She says kindness does not need a licence, and I have stopped arguing.
Oldric carried the last bier of Ahn-Solis on his shoulders as a boy. He will not say what was on it. I think he knows, and I think it hurts him.
Rue sings at the pond every dusk. Her voice breaks on the high note. The pilgrims weep, and I do not believe it is the song alone.
Gosse stocks the shelves and tells every customer the price is final. It has changed four times since the new moon, and she has never once been wrong.
Varrow keeps the Last Lamp lit all night. A sleeper wakes, sees the lamp and knows the room again. It is the whole of his art.
A rare trader paused at the pond once, in the dead of winter, and sold me a bell that rings without a clapper. I hang it by the door. It rings when somebody I have forgotten is nearby.
Go up by the climb. The rider holds the bowl of rock above it, and he has been waiting for lightning longer than he knows. Do not let him choose the ground.
The summit is cold, and the bier predates the temple. Once you face the Chancellor, say my name. He will pretend he does not remember it. He remembers every name.
A shadow crossed the pond at noon and the ice cracked into a handprint. Whether that was your doing or his, it was kind.
The lanterns burn without wind. Pilgrims have started to speak in full sentences. It will take a month to learn the sound of ordinary talk again.
A creature roosts in the cave south of the road, half wyvern and half harpy, with a voice that lulls whole flocks. Harl calls it a galewing. I call it a hazard.
Go gently into whatever lies below. You are not an empty vessel, whatever he said. You are a lamp still waiting to be told to shine.

senna_vey.name: Senna Vey
senna_vey.personality: hollow-eyed, courteous, bone-tired; answers questions slowly, as if translating from a language she is forgetting
senna_vey.voice: short exhausted sentences that trail off; listing what she has lost in the order she lost it

lines.text: I started in the south, with a husband and a mule. The mule lasted to the river. The husband lasted to the pass. I am the part that remained.
A pilgrim learns to measure by braziers. Three braziers, one hymn. Nine braziers, one night. A year is a very long row of fires.
Grey wool is warm enough if you stop caring about the rest of you. I am sorry. That is a strange thing to confess to a stranger.
The wyverns come down on the road at dusk to drink from the pond. We keep still. If you are still enough, they take you for a statue and do you no harm.
A man with a lance flew over us last week. He looked down at the camp. I think he was counting. I think he was sad.
I have a letter I mean to deliver. I do not recall to whom. The ink has run and the seal has gone to powder. I still carry it. A burden you cannot name is the easiest to keep.
Swordsman, you look like my husband before the pass. He would have shouldered the whole world and asked for a second helping.
Caster, the stars are wrong this far north. I used to steer by them. Now I steer by the soup.
Scout, there is a way off the road through the pines, a deer-track. I used to think I would take it. I have been thinking so for a year.
Priest, will you sit with me a while? You do not have to say anything. A person's company is a prayer if you let it be.
The abbot sits beside me and says nothing, and the nothing is the kindest thing anyone has given me since the mule.
Harl sketched a wyvern's wing for me. Every feather had a name. I learned three and forgot them, and he was gentle about it.
Ilka washes my feet every second night. I tell her not to. She says the feet are not mine to refuse. I have given up the argument.
Oldric tells me the bier road is only a road. I find that comforting. A road ends somewhere. A grief, they say, does not.
Rue sings a song I half-know. It is about a field of lamps. I hum the verse and she sings the rest, and we pretend it is a duet.
Gosse parted with a pair of needles. I have knit nothing. I carry them like a pair of small promises.
Varrow leaves a cup of milk by my bed. I do not drink milk. I keep the cup warm in my hands until the morning, and that is the use of it.
Into my hands a rare trader put a little glass bird, and said it would find its way home. It has not moved. Perhaps it is already there.
If you climb, tell the rider the road is long. He might like to hear that. He has the look of a man who thinks it is short.
They say the white man on the bier counts the stars and finds one missing every night. To be the star he finds would be worth any price.
The braziers all flared green for a moment, then settled. I sat very still. Something had been taken off my back that I had forgotten was there.
I went down to the pond's rim this morning. I only meant to look. I am going to take the deer-track at noon, and I have not decided what I will do at the end of it.
A creature in the south cave sings with two voices. One a hawk's, one a woman's. Flocks go to sleep on the wing when it sings. I have heard them fall.
Thank you for stopping. Most do not. It is a kindness to stop, even when there is nothing to be done.

harl_dunmore.name: Harl Dunmore
harl_dunmore.personality: lanky, wind-burned, enthusiastic to the point of danger; speaks of lethal animals with open affection
harl_dunmore.voice: field-notebook precision with sudden gusts of wonder; wingspans, thermals, hours of flight

lines.text: A full-grown wyvern has a wingspan of thirty feet and a bite force I have measured with a very expensive and now broken scale.
They nest in the roosts above the road and hunt along the thermals at dawn. I have logged four hundred flights. I know every one by its tail.
Whelps cause the most trouble. They are small enough to be reckless and large enough to be fatal, like the young of any species with an opinion of itself.
Their breath is a fire that comes up from a gland behind the throat. A dry night makes it worse. A wet one dampens it. I once timed a whelp's flame at eleven seconds. It cooked my notebook.
Wyverns fear lightning above all things. They have no way of grounding the charge in the wing. A bolt takes the whole beast to the floor, in one go, with a very surprised expression.
The rider is an exception. He does not fly like a person who is afraid. He flies like a person who has been told to stop being afraid, and has complied.
Swordsman, do not swing at a flying wyvern. You will miss, and the beast will laugh. Wait for it to land, or give it a reason.
Caster, a storm spell on the wing is the sole argument they respect. Hit the root of the wing. The whole body follows.
Scout, I need a sketch of a wyvern's underwing, drawn from life. I will pay in anything I own. The only condition is that you come back to hand it over.
Priest, would you bless my notebook? I have lost two to fire and one to a very rude thermal. A holy one might last.
The abbot lets me use the cellar for specimens. It is cold and quiet and he has never once asked what is in the jars.
Senna asked me to describe a wyvern's flight. I did, and she wept, and I could not tell what I had said. I think I described freedom.
Ilka patches me up each time a whelp gets too affectionate. She says I bleed like a man who enjoys it. She is not wrong.
Oldric tells me wyverns once drew the biers of the saints. I find that hard to believe and wonderful in about equal parts.
Rue composed a song about the roost for me. It lives in the lid of my notebook. The chorus says I am a fool. It rhymes beautifully.
Gosse refuses to stock wyvern scales, on principle. She says it is bad luck. I buy them anyway, from the hunters, and keep them under the bed.
Varrow told me the roost hums whenever the north wind blows. I went to listen. It does. It is a low D, and it is very close to a growl.
A rare trader once handed me an egg the size of a fist, and warned me not to let it hatch. It has been in my coat for a year. It is warm. It has never moved, and I check it every night.
The rider's wyvern is the oldest I have catalogued. Forty winters, at least. It does not breathe fire any more. It breathes ash. That tells you something about what it has seen.
I watched the rider fall from the ridge. I wept. I want you to know I was ashamed of how much of it was scientific interest.
The wyverns have gone quiet. Not gone, only quiet. They sit on the ridge with folded wings and look at the pond. No wyvern has ever looked at anything so long.
A whelp landed on my shoulder this morning and went to sleep. It is warm and it smells of woodsmoke. I will not move for a week.
Down south off the road lies a cave, a roost, and something in it that sings. A hybrid of wyvern and harpy: I have only ever heard it. Its breath puts a flock to sleep in mid-air.
If you ever meet a wyvern and it does not try to kill you, count it a gift. Write it down. I will want the date.

sister_ilka.name: Sister Ilka
sister_ilka.role: nurse of the long house, belongs to no order
sister_ilka.personality: square-shouldered, quiet, immovably kind; scrubs, boils and bandages as a form of prayer
sister_ilka.voice: bedside manner and clinical plainness; says the worst thing in the gentlest possible voice, then offers broth

lines.text: The long house has twenty beds and thirty-one patients. Some of them sleep on the floor and refuse to be moved. I have stopped trying.
A wyvern's sting festers. I boil the wound with salt and wrap it in lichen. It works a little more often than it fails.
Frostbite is quiet, like the road. A toe goes white and then goes away. I count a patient's toes the way other people count their prayers.
A curse from the dark knights is a slow ache. It does not leave a mark. It leaves a weariness that spreads. Warm broth and a little humour is the best cure.
Pilgrims arrive worn through at the soul as well as the boots. I cannot mend the soul. I can mend the boots and say nothing, and sometimes that is enough.
I was a washerwoman in Brinewick. I came north because somebody had to wash the road. It was an honest trade, and I never found the end of the laundry.
Swordsman, sit. I want a look at that shoulder. You are carrying a sprain you have been calling a habit.
Caster, your hands shake when you stop casting. That is the aftermath of spellwork. Drink something warm and hold the cup with both hands.
Scout, there is a sore on your heel you think nobody noticed. I noticed. Tell me how it got there and let me dress it.
Priest, you and I have the same job from different ends. You tend the part of a person that does not break. I tend the part that does.
The abbot visits the long house at midnight and prays by the window. He thinks I am asleep. I let him think so.
Senna has not slept more than an hour at a stretch since she arrived. I give her a warm stone for her feet and a hand to hold. I think the stone helps.
Harl comes in after every whelp encounter looking as though a hedge had beaten him. He is delighted every time. I am a little tired of it.
Oldric's knees have not been good since the bier. He refuses a cushion. I leave one on his chair, and he sits on it and denies it.
Rue sings to the dying. Only then does her voice hold steady. I think it knows what it is for.
Gosse keeps a drawer of bandages under the counter and will not charge for them. If anyone asks, they are a loan. Nobody has ever repaid one.
Varrow brings me a hot brick when I am up at three. He does not say a word, and the brick is always wrapped in flannel.
A rare trader brought me a salve once that smelled of snow, and took no payment. I used it on a child's burn. The scar faded by morning. I have been afraid of it since.
If the climb leaves you wounded, come straight here. I will not ask what happened. I will ask where it hurts, and I will believe the answer.
I patched a grey scarf this morning, one the rider left on the road. It is very well made. I cannot think what to do with it, so I keep it folded on the shelf.
The long house is quiet tonight. Several patients stirred in their sleep and said names. Each name was somebody who had been waiting.
Eight of my thirty-one are well enough to walk to the pond. They stood there in the snow and looked at the lanterns and none of them said a word.
A voice rises from the south cave, and the wind carries it down the road. Three of my patients have slept through the night to it. I cannot decide if that is a cure or a lure.
Rest when you can, eat when you must, and let somebody wash your boots. There is no heroism in a blister.

oldric_bearer.name: Oldric the Bearer
oldric_bearer.role: retired bier-bearer, last of the temple's pall-carriers
oldric_bearer.personality: gruff, ancient, immovable; talks about carrying as other men talk about God
oldric_bearer.voice: weights and distances; every anecdote is measured in paces; refuses sentiment and delivers it anyway

lines.text: Eight bearers to a bier, four on each side. I carried the left rear pole for sixty years. It is a good place. You never see the face, only the weight.
A bier is a bed for a very long sleep. The poles were cut from ash, and the cloth was grey wool, and the pace was always the same. Slow. A thing you carry should not be hurried.
I was ten when I lifted my first. It was a saint of the temple, light as a bundle of reeds. The elder bearers said the lightest ones are the heaviest. They were right.
The road was paved for the biers. Every step you take on it was cut for a foot shod in felt, going slowly, with a lantern ahead and a bell behind.
Wyverns drew the great biers in the old days, one on each side, wings folded. A wyvern with a harness is a quiet thing. The man on the bier did not mind the speed. He had nowhere left to be.
I do not talk about the last bier. I will say only that the pole bent, and that the woman who followed it did not weep.
Swordsman, a good shoulder is worth a good sword. Lift with the legs and never the back. It is the oldest craft there is.
Caster, the great biers had a rune cut into the foot of each pole. It kept the load steady. I could not read it. I could always feel it.
Scout, there is a short way through the pines, a bearer's cut, used when the road was iced. It saves an hour and costs a skinned knee. I recommend it.
Priest, you may wish to say a few words at the summit. The old rite is short. Name the dead, name the road, and say that you carried them as far as you could.
The abbot was an acolyte when I was a bearer. He walked ahead with the bell. He had a beautiful voice. He does not use it any more.
Senna warms herself at the third brazier. I carried a woman like her once, only she was lighter. I wish I had said something to the bundle.
Harl asks me whether a wyvern ever pulled a bier at a trot. I tell him no. He writes it down and looks disappointed. I lacked the nerve to say I was joking.
Ilka has the strongest back I have ever seen on a woman. She would have made a good bearer. I told her so, and she said she would rather carry the living.
Rue sings the bearers' hymn at the pond, the one with the long slow verses. I used to sing it under my breath at the rear pole. Hearing it from outside is a very strange thing.
Gosse sells a rope I could not break in my prime. I bought three coils. A bearer who is not prepared has no business near a hill.
Varrow never charges me for the inn. He says the Last Lamp owes the bearers a bed. I have never contradicted him, as it is the one point on which I agree with a stranger.
Once a rare trader held out a shoulder-pad that spreads weight perfectly across the back. I declined. It would have felt like cheating, and it would have been an insult to the poles.
The last bier went up the climb on the new moon, drawn by wyverns, and no bearers walked beside it. A bier with no bearers is a thing that has made up its mind.
I watched the rider come down. A wyvern settles like a boat on a lake. A rider who has stopped believing settles like a stone. This one went down like a stone.
The bier is empty now, they say. It always was. That is the part nobody told the bearers. We carried nothing for sixty years, and nothing weighed exactly as much as it should.
I laid down my pole tonight, in my mind, for the last time. It is a strange feeling. Like putting down a very old friend who has stopped needing to be held.

South of the road, in the roost, a creature has grown up from a pair of old bloodlines: wyvern and harpy. Its song carries over the pines. It is the only music I have heard in forty years that sounded like a bier.
Walk like you are carrying something precious, because you are. The pace does not matter. Only the care.

cantor_rue.name: Cantor Rue
cantor_rue.role: pond-side singer who leads the evening hymn
cantor_rue.personality: slight, bright-eyed, trembling just under the surface; a voice like a cracked bell and a laugh like a dropped spoon
cantor_rue.voice: verses, refrains and key signatures; mentions the note of every object in the room

lines.text: A hymn needs three things: a tune, a reason, and somebody to cry quietly in the back row. We have the first two in abundance.
The evening hymn has fourteen verses and nobody remembers more than six. I make up the rest on the spot. Last Thursday I rhymed grief with beef. The abbot forgave me.
The pond rings when it freezes. A very low note, almost beneath hearing. I tune to it each dusk. It is flat by a quarter-tone and I love it more for that.
A wyvern sings, you know, when it is happy. A deep rolling hum that shakes the ice. I have sung back. We hold a harmony for as long as the breath allows.
The old bearers' hymn has a rest in the fourth bar where the pace changes. A person who has carried a bier can feel it in their shoulder. I have it in my throat.
I came north because my teacher died and left me a lute with a cracked belly. It sounds better than it should. I think it is grateful to be useful.
Swordsman, you hum when you march. I heard you from the road. A low G, a little sharp. If you do not mind, I would like to borrow it for a verse.
Caster, a spell is a song with a purpose. Have you ever tried singing the words instead of speaking them? It changes nothing about the fire and much about the mood.
Scout, the wind carries sound farther than you would guess. Next time you creep up on somebody, hum a note and see if they turn around.
Priest, join the evening hymn. I need a second voice on the descant, and a voice that has actually meant the words.
The abbot has the best bass in the north and he refuses to use it. I leave a verse empty each night in case he changes his mind.
Senna hums along sometimes, without opening her mouth. I keep a space for her in every chorus, and I never look in her direction.
Harl asked me for a roost ballad. I wrote one. It has eleven verses and the rhymes are mostly wing and sting and king. He has it framed.
Ilka hums a very flat B while she scrubs. It is the most restful sound I know. I tuned the long house to it, and the patients sleep better.
Oldric sings the bearers' hymn under his breath in the dark. I pretend not to hear and I match his pitch from across the room.
Gosse has a laugh like a brass pot. It is the only cheerful note in the halt and I have written three songs around it.
Varrow whistles a single phrase every night when he closes up. It goes up and does not come down. A year of effort has not resolved it.
A rare trader once gave me a tuning fork of a metal I could not name. It rings at a pitch just above hearing. When I strike it, the pond shivers.
If you climb the road tonight, sing something. The rider listens to the wind and the wind carries the tune. He may not stop, but he will hear it.
I wrote a verse for the rider. Four lines about a man who learned to land. Do not tell him. I do not know how it ends.
The note of the pond changed at noon. It went up by a half-step and stayed there. I stood at the shore for an hour, trying to hold it in my throat.
Tonight we sing all fourteen verses, and I have written the missing eight. It took three days, a quart of tea and an argument with a crow. The last verse is about you.
Something sings in the south cave: two voices in perfect fifths, one rough and one clear. A galewing, Harl says. I have tried to match it and failed. I will keep trying.
May your road have a melody and your rests be well placed. That is the only blessing a cantor has, and I give it with all my cracked heart.

gosse_marr.name: Gosse Marr
gosse_marr.personality: short, forceful, unsentimental; her brass laugh is the loudest thing in the halt
gosse_marr.voice: haggling as performance art; prices stated like verdicts and revised like weather

say: Gosse Marr. Mourners' Provisions. The price is final. Unless it is not, in which case it has been revised, and I will explain why in great detail.
Stone salve for gaze, silver oil for ghosts, clear tea against curses, and a very reasonable line in phoenix plumes. I do not stock wyvern scales. They are bad luck, and I will not hear otherwise.

lines.text: A fair price is the one at which both parties leave unhappy. By that measure I run the fairest shop in the north.
Everything on this shelf came up the road on a mule or a back. Count the stairs when you think of the price.
I have sold eleven hundred candles this winter. Not one of them was bought by a cheerful person. It is a grim trade and a steady one.
A phoenix plume costs what it costs. If it brings back one friend, it has paid for itself. If it brings back two, I would like a cut.
Grand elixir cures four ailments and sells for three hundred. I once tried selling a five-ailment version. It proved to be cheese.
My ledger has a column for the dead. I enter their debts and strike them out. No other accounting I know is so honest.
Swordsman, a hard road wears a blade down. Whetstones are by the till, a good one at a bad price, which is the only kind I carry.
Caster, I stock ether by the flask. A tired mind is an expensive thing, and I can offer a very reasonable rate for the repair.
Scout, the rope behind the counter holds a ton and weighs a pound. It costs more than it should and I refuse to apologise.
Priest, candles are half price for the chapel. Ask me why and I will say business. It is mostly a lie, and I would like to keep it.
The abbot owes me for forty loaves. He has never paid and I have never asked. Between us it passes for a tithe.
Senna buys one needle a week and never uses it. A whole drawer holds her needles. Someday I will give her the lot, and she will cry, and I will blame the dust.
Harl pays in sketches. His drawings of wyverns hang in the back room. They are remarkably good and utterly unsellable.
Ilka takes her bandages and tries to pay with scrubbing. I let her scrub the floor. It has never been cleaner. Service has never been better.
Oldric buys rope and never haggles. It is a little unnerving. A man who accepts the price either respects me or has given up on prices, and neither is a good sign.
Rue is always ten coppers short and always pays in a verse. I keep the verses in a jar. The jar is nearly full.
Varrow buys lamp oil by the cask and swears it is for the lamps. It is, mostly. A little of it goes into a sort of pastry. Do not ask.
Scales that weigh grief were left to me by a rare trader. I put a candle on one pan and a loaf on the other. The loaf won. I have not used them since.
The road to the climb costs more than the road from the camp. Buy salve before you go. A wyvern's breath is cheaper to dodge than to treat.
The Chancellor's bier stands on the summit, and no one has dared to price it. Should you come on a crate with my brand on the lid, I will give you a very honest discount.
I raised no prices today. I have been selling candles for a fortnight at cost. People ask why. I tell them it is a promotion. It is not.
I have decided to open a second shelf. Seeds, mostly. The pond is thawing early and the pilgrims have started to talk about planting.
Hunters offer me galewing feathers now and then. I turn them down. A feather like that should be on a hat or in a river. It should not be on a shelf.
Final price, final farewell. Come back soon and complain. I will miss the arguing.

varrow_pike.name: Varrow Pike
varrow_pike.role: keeper of the Last Lamp inn
varrow_pike.personality: long, unhurried, courteous; a man who has learned to stay awake for a living and to enjoy it
varrow_pike.voice: wicks, shutters, night-watches; every sentence has the cadence of a lamp being trimmed

say: Varrow Pike. This is the Last Lamp. One hundred and forty a night, a clean bed and a lantern that stays lit until you wake.
The lamp is the entirety of my art. A sleeper wakes in a strange place, sees a light, and remembers where he is. That is all the comfort I know how to give, and it is usually enough.

lines.text: A lamp in a window says two things: someone is awake, and the road is not empty. Both are worth the price of the oil.
I trim the wick at the fourth hour, when the night is thinnest. A trimmed flame burns blue at the root, and a guest who sees it dreams of water.
The inn has nine beds and one rule. Nobody is turned away, and nobody is asked why. I have housed a duke and a deserter in the same room.
Wyverns will not roost near a lantern. It is the one useful thing I have learned about them. Keep the flame steady and the sky leaves you alone.
A curse breaks over breakfast. It takes a hot meal, a window, and a person to say good morning. Nobody has ever failed to recover on good morning.
Once I lit lamps in the city. I came north for a quieter flame, and I found one. It is the only light on the road, and it is mine.
Swordsman, I have set a rack by your bed for the blade. A weapon that rests near its owner sleeps lightly. I find it a comfort.
Caster, there is a draught in room three that smells of ozone. I think a spell lodged in the wall. If you can unpick it, the bed is yours for free.
Scout, the shutter in room five opens onto the roof. A person with a quiet foot can reach the pines from there. I leave the latch loose when I trust the guest.
Priest, the abbot says the Last Lamp is the only chapel the road still needs. I would be honoured if you blessed the wick.
Hale Corvane takes the corner seat in my common room every Friday and says not a word. I leave him a pot of tea and a plate of sugared bread. It has become a rite.
Senna sleeps in the end bed, upright, with her boots on. I leave a blanket folded at her feet. By daylight it lies unfolded.
Harl keeps a ledger of wyvern flights on my kitchen table. I do not move it. A good notebook in a good light is a sort of company.
Ilka comes in at three for hot water. She never asks. The kettle goes on at a quarter to, and she is always grateful and never says why.
Oldric takes the bed nearest the stairs so he can hear the whole inn breathe. He has been at it for forty years. It is a bearer's habit.
Rue practises in the cellar. The floorboards carry it up. Some nights the bass notes rattle the cups, and I let them.
Gosse sends me oil at cost and grumbles over it all week. I send back a loaf. The loaf wins the argument every time.
A rare trader once spent a night in my best room and left behind a lantern with a green flame. It has burned for two years and never needed oil. It sits down in the cellar and I avoid its eye.
If the climb goes badly, come back to the lamp. It will be lit. It is always lit. That is the whole point of it.
The rider's wyvern was seen circling the inn three nights running. It never landed. I hung an extra lantern in the east window. It seemed to help.
All the pond lanterns lit themselves at noon, and mine burned a little greener. I am going to pretend I saw nothing, because it was beautiful.
All nine beds are taken. A man tried to pay me in thanks, and I let him. It is a good coin and it keeps no matter the weather.
The south cave hums at night whenever the east wind blows. Two voices, one clear and one rough. I set a lantern at the sill facing it. I think it likes the company.
Sleep well, and wake to a light you recognise. That is all my hospitality amounts to, and it has not once proved enough, and it has not once amounted to nothing.
